author: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi
biz: Match the difficulty to the adviser, and let them see how they did

Flow needs a challenge just above current skill plus immediate feedback. This week, grade incoming enquiries at HomeownersLoan and Apply4Loan by complexity and route the harder cases to your more experienced advisers rather than by whoever is free. Then give every adviser a same day signal that is about quality rather than pressure: whether the customer could restate the key facts, whether the suitability notes are complete, whether anything needed correcting. Measure call quality scores, first time accuracy of fact finds, and complaints. Never a target that rewards pushing a customer who should be told no.
Give a distressed client one clear next step

Csikszentmihalyi's two failure states are boredom and anxiety, and people arriving at Debt Support Direct are deep in the second: the challenge is enormous and their sense of skill is nil. Anxiety eats attention, so they absorb almost nothing you say. This week, end every first conversation with one achievable action, stated plainly, written down and sent to them, with a named person and a date to confirm it is done. Measure the share of first appointments that end with a completed next step, and how many clients return for the second conversation.

b: He was born on the twenty ninth of September 1934 in Fiume, a port on the Adriatic that belonged to Italy then and is called Rijeka in Croatia now. His father was a Hungarian diplomat at the consulate there. The family spoke Hungarian at home, Italian in the street and German when it was useful, and the boy, the third son, grew up between Fiume, Florence and Rome as though that arrangement were permanent.

It was not. By 1944 Hungary had become a battlefield. One of his two older half brothers was killed in the siege of Budapest, when Mihaly was ten. The other, Moricz, was taken by the Soviet army and sent to a labour camp in Siberia, and the brothers would not see each other again for decades. Friends and relatives in Budapest were killed. Reference accounts of his life say that the boy himself spent a period in an Italian prison camp, although not every account of those years mentions it.

What he remembered was not heroism. It was the sight of adults coming apart. People he had trusted lost their work, their standing and their sense of who they were, and a good number of them never got any of it back. Others, in exactly the same ruins, stayed somehow whole. That contrast became the question he spent the next sixty years answering.

And he remembered chess. He played it through the worst of it, and he said later that he discovered chess was a miraculous way of entering into a different world where all those things did not matter.

Hold on to that image, because the whole book is inside it. A chessboard offers a small closed world with clear rules, instant feedback and a difficulty you can just about meet. While a child sits over one, attention is entirely used up, and a mind that is entirely used up has no room left over for fear. He would spend his career showing that this was not escape. It was the ordinary machinery of a good hour.

b: After the war his father was appointed Hungarian ambassador to Italy and the family moved to Rome. It lasted barely two years. When the communists took power in Hungary at the end of the 1940s his father resigned rather than serve them, and the new government answered by dismissing him and stripping the family of its citizenship.

So they stayed in Rome as refugees and did what refugees do. They opened a restaurant. A man they took on turned out to be a swindler and walked off with the family savings. Mihaly left school to bring money in, worked as a travel agent and then as a news photographer, and painted in whatever hours were left.

He was about sixteen when he went to Switzerland and found himself with no money for an evening out. There was a free public lecture advertised on the subject of flying saucers, so he went to that. The speaker was Carl Jung, and the talk was not really about saucers at all. It was about a traumatised continent and the delusions a frightened population will reach for. That struck me, he said afterwards, and it is one of the few moments in his life he described as a hinge.

He began reading Jung, then Freud. And the question that had been forming since the war finally had words. Not what breaks people, but what keeps some of them intact. He had met Hungarians who had come back from the Soviet camps and seemed, oddly, at peace, while men who had lost far less were wrecked for good.
There was one obstacle. In the Europe of the early 1950s psychology was barely a university subject. If he wanted to study it properly he would have to cross the Atlantic.

b: He arrived in Chicago in 1956, aged twenty two, with a dollar and twenty five cents and very little English. He picked up the language partly from Pogo comic books borrowed from American servicemen, which is a strange way to learn a tongue and left him with an ear for the idiom. He took a job as a night auditor in a hotel downtown, adding up the day's takings while the city slept, and enrolled at the University of Chicago.

The psychology he found was not the psychology he had come for. American departments were busy with rats, reflexes and behaviour you could count, and the inner life was treated as either unmeasurable or beside the point. He had crossed an ocean to ask what makes a life worth living and been handed a maze.

He stayed anyway, partly because he found a precedent in Abraham Maslow, who was writing about people at their best rather than their worst. A scholarship came in his junior year. He graduated in 1959, stayed on for a doctorate under Jacob Getzels, and finished it in 1965.

The lesson of those years is worth stealing. If the field you have joined studies only what is broken, the interesting questions are the ones nobody is asking. He decided to study excellent moments rather than damaged ones, which in 1960 looked like an eccentric career move and in hindsight looks like the entire point.
ch.cap: Night auditor by night, student by day
ch.h: One dollar and twenty five cents

b: His doctoral work took him into the studios of young painters at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. He wanted to know how creative problems are found and solved, so he sat and watched them paint, hour after hour, and wrote down what he saw.

What he saw was almost physical. A painter would go into the work and effectively disappear. Hunger, thirst, tiredness, the time of day, all of it stopped registering. The picture was going badly and then well in small increments, each stroke answering the one before, and nothing outside the edge of the canvas existed at all.

Then came the detail that made the career. When a canvas was finished, most of them lost interest in it almost at once. They would turn it to face the wall, stack it with the others and start another one. Whatever they had been chasing was not the object, and it was not the applause either. It was the hours.

In the psychology of the day this made very little sense. Behaviour was supposed to be pulled along by rewards outside itself: money, status, approval, food. Here were people paying a real price in order to spend time in a particular state of mind, and then discarding the reward at the end. The activity carried its own purpose. He later borrowed a pair of Greek words for it and called such things autotelic, from self and goal, meaning an activity whose aim is itself.
If you have ever stayed up to finish something nobody asked you for, and felt better the next morning than you do after an easy evening, you already know what he was looking at.

b: Through the early 1970s he and his students went looking for the state in the wild. They interviewed rock climbers, chess players, dancers, basketball players, composers, surgeons and people on assembly lines, anyone who did something difficult for reasons that were not obviously practical.

The surprise was how alike the answers were. A climber on a rock face and a surgeon at a table described the same handful of things. Attention narrowing until only the task was left. The nagging inner commentary about how one was doing going quiet. A feeling of control that cost no effort. And time behaving oddly, hours passing in what felt like minutes, or a single second stretching out.

They also kept reaching for the same metaphor. It was like being carried along by a current. It flowed. He took the word from them, which is why the term is a piece of plain English rather than jargon. The first book came in 1975, titled Beyond Boredom and Anxiety, and that title names the two banks of the river.

Out of the interviews came the conditions, and these are the practical core of everything he ever wrote. A flow activity has goals clear enough that you always know what to do next. It gives feedback immediately, so you can tell at once whether you are doing it well. And its difficulty sits a little above your present skill, high enough to demand everything you have, low enough that you have a chance.

Get those three right and absorption tends to follow. Too easy, and attention wanders off into boredom. Too hard, and it curdles into anxiety. Much of the misery of ordinary work, he argued, is a difficulty setting problem wearing the costume of a motivation problem.

b: Interviews have a flaw. People remember their lives better or worse than they lived them, and by the time you ask, the moment has been rewritten. So his laboratory built a way of catching experience while it was still happening. Volunteers carried an electronic pager and a small booklet. At random moments the thing went off, and they wrote down where they were, what they were doing, what they were thinking about, and how they felt on a few simple scales.

It is called the experience sampling method, and it is one of the quietly important inventions of twentieth century psychology. The doctoral work of Suzanne Prescott, one of his students, is credited with developing it, with Mihaly supervising, and the early studies carried the names of Reed Larson and Ronald Graef alongside his own. In 1985 he and Larson published Being Adolescent, built on beeping seventy five American teenagers through their ordinary weeks.

Tens of thousands of these snapshots turned a philosophical idea into data. Flow could be counted. It was frequent in some lives and nearly absent from others. It arrived most reliably in activities with rules and feedback, which is to say sport, music, craft, serious conversation and demanding work. It almost never arrived in front of a television, which people nevertheless chose for hours at a time.

That last finding is the uncomfortable one. Asked what they wanted, people reliably named rest. Measured in the moment, rest left them flatter than effort did. The gap between what we predict will feel good and what actually does is wide enough to swallow an evening, and then a decade.

b: In 1989, with Judith LeFevre, he published the finding that ought to have changed the way we talk about jobs. They beeped seventy eight adult workers for a week and sorted every snapshot twice over, by whether the person was working or at leisure, and by whether they were in flow.

Flow mattered more than the difference between work and leisure on almost every measure of how good the moment felt. And the great majority of flow experiences were reported at work. Jobs, it turns out, are where most adults actually meet clear goals, immediate feedback and a difficulty that stretches them.

Then the twist. In those same absorbed moments at work, people still said they would rather be somewhere else. Motivation ran higher in leisure even when leisure felt worse. We want to be off, and we feel best when we are on.

He did not conclude that everyone should work more. He concluded that we are poor judges of our own experience, and that both halves of life are badly designed. Work is arranged to produce absorption only by accident. Free time is often arranged to produce nothing whatsoever. Mending either is a matter of putting goals, feedback and the right level of difficulty where they are missing, which is cheaper than it sounds and almost nobody does on purpose.

b: The book that gathered all of this appeared in 1990 from Harper and Row, under the title Flow, with the subtitle The Psychology of Optimal Experience. It sold more than three hundred thousand copies within about two years, which for a work of academic psychology is a small earthquake. Bill Clinton and Tony Blair both said they had read it, and Jimmy Johnson used it with the Dallas Cowboys before the Super Bowl of 1993.

Its argument starts with a hard limit. Attention is finite. He put the figure at roughly a hundred and twenty six bits of information a second, a number he had borrowed from an engineer, and whatever the true quantity may be the point survives. Everything you experience has to pass through a narrow channel. Attention is therefore not a mood or a virtue. It is the only currency you have, and your life consists of what you spend it on.

When that channel fills up with conflicting demands, threats to your standing and the running question of how you are doing, he called the result psychic entropy, which is simply disorder in consciousness. Flow is the opposite condition, order in consciousness, and it feels good for an almost mechanical reason. There is no attention left over for anything to go wrong in.

Around that he set out the components, eight or so depending on how you count them: clear goals, immediate feedback, challenge matched to skill, action and awareness merging, complete concentration, a sense of control, the disappearance of self consciousness, and the distortion of time. He drew the famous channel running between boredom and anxiety, and pointed out that it slides. Today's stretch is next month's routine, so the only way to stay in the channel is to keep raising the difficulty. That, he argued, is how flow grows a person rather than merely entertaining one.

And he refused the easy version of his own idea. Flow is morally empty. A burglar at a lock, a soldier in a raid and a gambler at a machine can all be deep inside it. The state tells you nothing about whether the activity deserves your hours, which is why the last part of the book is not about technique at all. It is about choosing a goal large enough to hold a life together, so that the time you spend absorbed adds up to something you would defend.

b: At the end of the 1990s he left Chicago after thirty years and moved to California as professor of psychology and management at Claremont Graduate University, where he founded the Quality of Life Research Center. With Martin Seligman he became one of the two founders of positive psychology, the attempt to study what goes right with the same rigour long reserved for what goes wrong.

Rigour cuts both ways, and it has cut into flow. In 2008 Stefan Engeser and Falko Rheinberg measured flow with an independent scale instead of defining it as high challenge plus high skill, and found the balance idea only partly supported. It held when the activity mattered to the person, and depended on their appetite for achievement. Reviews of the measurement, notably by Giovanni Moneta in 2012, found that the eight components do not hang together as one clean state. Concentration, control and the merging of action and awareness belong together. Clear goals and feedback behave like causes. Altered time and enjoyment behave like consequences.

A scoping review of two hundred and fifty two flow studies published in 2022 by Corinna Peifer and colleagues reached a fair verdict. The experience is real and described consistently, the evidence is mostly correlational and self reported, and the link between flow and performance is mixed. The widely quoted claim that flow makes people five times more productive cannot be traced to any defensible study. The critic Oliver James dismissed the whole idea as tautology. And researchers studying slot machine players now write about dark flow, absorption that works exactly as advertised and ruins the person having it, which is the moral emptiness Mihaly himself had insisted on.
He died at home in Claremont on the twentieth of October 2021, aged eighty seven, survived by his wife Isabella, an editor he had worked alongside for sixty years, and their two sons.

What survives is not the diagram. It is the instruction, and it needs no laboratory. Notice the hours you lose yourself in, and ask what the conditions were. Almost always you will find a clear goal, quick feedback and a difficulty just past your skill. Then build more days out of those and fewer out of the evenings you cannot remember. The boy with the chessboard had been right about the door. The rest of his life was spent working out where the hinges were.

connects: Ericsson's deliberate practice sits in the same narrow band just above current skill, but he insists it is usually not enjoyable, which is the sharpest challenge to Csikszentmihalyi's claim that the stretch itself feels good.
Newport's deep work is largely an engineering manual for the conditions Csikszentmihalyi only described: protect the attention, remove the interruptions, raise the difficulty.

Frankl and Csikszentmihalyi came out of the same ruined Europe asking why some survivors stayed whole, and answered with meaning and with order in consciousness, which are closer to each other than either man's vocabulary suggests.
note: Dates, posts and publication details follow the standard reference accounts of his life, the University of Chicago obituary of October 2021 and his own books. The quotation about chess, the remark that the Jung lecture struck him and the detail of arriving with a dollar and twenty five cents come from interviews and profiles rather than documents, so they are his own version of events. Reference works state that he spent a period in an Italian prison camp as a child, and some accounts of his early life omit it, so it is given here with that caveat; sources also differ on whether his first degree was awarded in 1959 or 1960. The figure of a hundred and twenty six bits a second was borrowed from engineering estimates and is now regarded as a loose extrapolation, and the later findings of Engeser and Rheinberg, Moneta and Peifer and colleagues are described as those researchers report them.
recall: Where did the word flow come from?

From the people he interviewed in the early 1970s. Climbers, chess players, dancers and surgeons kept describing the state as being carried along by a current, and he adopted their metaphor. That is why the term is plain English rather than technical jargon.
What are the three conditions that produce flow?

Clear goals, so you always know what to do next. Immediate feedback, so you can tell at once how you are doing. And a challenge pitched just above your current skill. Too little challenge gives boredom, too much gives anxiety.
What is the experience sampling method?

Volunteers carry a pager and a booklet, and at random moments record what they are doing and how they feel. It was developed in his Chicago laboratory in the 1970s, credited to the doctoral work of his student Suzanne Prescott, with Reed Larson and Ronald Graef on the early studies.
What did Csikszentmihalyi and LeFevre find in 1989?

They sampled seventy eight adult workers for a week and found that most flow experiences happened at work rather than in leisure. Yet in those same moments people said they would rather be elsewhere, and reported higher motivation during leisure.
What did he mean by psychic entropy?

Disorder in consciousness, caused by attention being pulled between conflicting demands and worries about the self. Flow is its opposite, order in consciousness, which feels good partly because no attention is left over for anything to go wrong in.
recap:
Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi was born in 1934 in Fiume, a port that was then Italian and is now Croatian, the third son of a Hungarian diplomat. The war took one half brother at the siege of Budapest and sent the other to Siberia, and the boy watched the adults around him come apart while a few stayed whole. He played chess through it, and said later that it was a miraculous way of entering a different world where none of that mattered. A chessboard gives you clear rules, instant feedback and a difficulty you can just about meet, and a mind entirely occupied has no room left for fear.

After the war his father resigned as ambassador rather than serve the communists, the family lost its citizenship and opened a restaurant in Rome, and Mihaly left school to earn. At about sixteen, in Switzerland, he wandered into a free lecture on flying saucers that turned out to be Carl Jung talking about a traumatised Europe, and decided to become a psychologist. In 1956 he arrived in Chicago with a dollar and twenty five cents, worked nights as a hotel auditor, and took his degree and then his doctorate there.

His doctoral work put him in painters' studios, where he saw people forget to eat for hours and then turn the finished canvas to the wall. The reward was the doing, not the object. In the early 1970s he and his students interviewed climbers, dancers, surgeons and chess players, who all described the same state and reached for the same word: it flowed. From them he took the conditions. Clear goals. Immediate feedback. A challenge just above your skill. Too little and you drift into boredom, too much and you tip into anxiety.

To measure it his laboratory built the experience sampling method: a pager, a booklet and random moments. Tens of thousands of snapshots showed that flow is common in some lives, nearly absent in others, and almost never comes from a television. In 1989, with Judith LeFevre, he found that most flow happens at work, and that people in those very moments still wished they were somewhere else. The book came in 1990. stories: The lecture that was not about flying saucers

In the early 1950s a teenage refugee was in Switzerland with no money for an evening out. He saw a free public lecture advertised on the subject of flying saucers and went in for something to do. The speaker was Carl Jung, and the talk turned out to be about a traumatised Europe and the delusions a frightened population reaches for. The boy had been chased out of Hungary by exactly that. He went home, read Jung, then Freud, and decided to become a psychologist. He later said simply that it struck him.
One dollar and twenty five cents

Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi arrived in Chicago in 1956 at the age of twenty two with a dollar and twenty five cents to his name and barely any English, which he improved by reading Pogo comic books borrowed from American servicemen. He took a job as a night auditor in a downtown hotel, totting up the day's takings while the city slept, and enrolled at the University of Chicago. Within a decade he was a doctor of psychology there. Within thirty years he had written the book that put the word flow into ordinary conversation.
The canvases turned to face the wall

For his doctorate he sat in the studios of young painters in Chicago and simply watched. They would vanish into the work for hours, forgetting food, drink and the time of day. Then, when a canvas was finished, most of them lost interest in it within minutes. They turned it to face the wall, stacked it with the rest and started another. Whatever they were chasing, it was not the object and it was not the applause. It was the hours. That observation became an entire career, and eventually a word everyone uses.
take: Attention is the only currency you have
Decide each morning on the one thing that deserves an uninterrupted hour, and remove the competing claims on it before you start. Your life is made of what you attend to, not what you intend.
Set the difficulty, not the mood
When work feels dull, raise the challenge. When it feels frightening, shrink the task or build the skill first. Motivation usually follows the difficulty setting rather than leading it.
Build in feedback you cannot ignore
Any task where you cannot tell how you are doing will drain you. Add a signal, a score, a check or a reader, so that every step answers the one before it.
Before you begin, write the next action precisely enough that you would know the moment it was done. Vagueness is where attention leaks away.
Rest is not the opposite of misery
Passive evenings reliably feel worse than demanding ones, however much you looked forward to them. Spend part of your free time on something with rules and feedback.
The channel slides, so keep raising it
What stretched you last year is this year's boredom. Add difficulty on purpose, or absorption will quietly disappear and you will blame your job.
Some work is worth doing for the hours
Judge a few activities by the time they give you rather than the object they leave behind. People who do that outlast people chasing only the result.
Being absorbed proves nothing about whether a thing deserves your life. Choose the goal on other grounds, then enjoy the state it gives you.
